title: Hunayn and at-Ta'if
year: 8 AH — Shawwal to Dhul-Qa'dah, 630 CE, the weeks after Makkah fell
era: The Largest Army He Ever Had, and It Ran
teaser: Twelve thousand men walked into a valley at dawn. Minutes later he was almost the only one facing forward.

layers.title: The Setting
layers.subtitle: A blind old man argues with a young chief
layers.content:
Makkah had fallen in Ramadan, and most of Arabia read the fall as final. Some tribes read it differently. Nasr, Jusham, Sa'd bin Bakr and the people of Bani Hilal — all of them from Qais Aylan, and behind them the two large blocs of Hawazin and Thaqif — held themselves too proud to admit a victory won by somebody else. They went to Malik bin Awf an-Nasri and made up their minds to fight.

Malik took his people out to Awtas, a valley in the lands of Hawazin near Hunayn, adjacent to Dhul-Majaz, some ten miles from Makkah in the direction of Arafat. He brought their wealth, their women and their children with them.

One man in the camp objected. Duraid bin as-Simmah was old and known across Arabia for his experience of war, and when the crowd carried him to Malik he asked first what valley they were in. Awtas, they said. Good ground for horses, he answered — no sharp height, no loose soil. Then why do I hear camels growling, donkeys braying, children crying, sheep bleating? They explained: Malik wants every family and every property behind the line, so the men will fight to protect them.

Duraid called Malik over and told him he was nothing but a shepherd. Do you believe anything on earth stops a man who has decided to run? If you win you have gained a man with a sword and a spear. If you lose you have handed over your people and your goods together. Put the families up where they are safe, mount the young men, and fight with those.

Malik refused. Hawazin obey me, he said, or I lean on this sword until it comes through my back. His people said: we obey you. Duraid answered that this was a day he had never missed in his life, and would not now be tempted to watch.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Valley Before Dawn
layers.subtitle: The biggest column he had ever led, broken in minutes
layers.content:
He marched out nineteen days after entering Makkah with twelve thousand men. Ten thousand had come up for the conquest; of the other two thousand, most were Makkans who had accepted Islam within the month. He borrowed a hundred suits of armour with their equipment from Safwan bin Umayyah and left Attab bin Asid in charge of the city. The dates as printed in the sirah do not agree with one another — the departure is given as Saturday the nineteenth of Shawwal and the arrival at Hunayn as the night of Wednesday the tenth, and the two cannot both stand.

On the road they passed a great green Nabk tree called Dhat Anwat. The Arabs used to visit it, hang their weapons on it and slaughter beside it. Some of the army asked him to make them one like it. Allah is the Greatest, he said. You have just said what the people of Moses said to him: make us a god as the one they have.

Others, looking down the length of the column, said: we shall not be defeated. That sentence fell hard on him.

Malik had entered the valley of Hunayn by night. He put his men inside it — along the roads, in the entrances, in the narrow places — and ordered them to open with stones and then charge all together.

In the dark before dawn the Muslims began descending into the valley, knowing nothing. As they started to pitch camp the arrows came down and the battalions came out of the rocks in one movement. The army broke. The rout was so total that Abu Sufyan bin Harb, a Muslim of a few weeks, said the retreat would not stop before the Red Sea.

The Prophet ﷺ turned to the right and called out that he was the Messenger of Allah, Muhammad the son of Abdullah, the grandson of Abdul-Muttalib. What stood with him was a few Emigrants and some of his own kin. The Sealed Nectar names Abu Sufyan at the rein of his mule and his uncle al-Abbas at the stirrup, both hauling to hold the animal still while he pushed it toward the enemy. Then he came down off it and asked: O Allah, send down Your help.
layers.hadith_ref: Jami' at-Tirmidhi and Musnad Ahmad — the tree called Dhat Anwat and 'you have said what the people of Moses said'
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Turning Point
layers.subtitle: One loud voice and a handful of dirt
layers.content:
Al-Abbas had a carrying voice. The Prophet ﷺ ordered him to use it.

Where are the lancers, he shouted. By Allah, al-Abbas said afterwards, when they heard me calling them back they turned round toward the fighting like wild cows tending to their calves. Here we are, they answered. Here we are. Men who could not force a camel to turn flung their armour round their necks, dropped off the animal with a weapon in hand and let it run loose. A hundred of them gathered round him and the battle restarted.

The next call was for the Ansar. O people of the Ansar. The last group summoned by name was Bani al-Harith bin al-Khazraj. The battalions poured back into the valley in the same order they had left it, and both sides stood and fought without giving ground.

Now the fight has grown fierce, he said, watching it. Then he took up a handful of dirt and threw it into the faces of the enemy: may your faces be shameful. Their eyes filled with dust and the line started to come apart.

Only a few hours separated that handful of dust from the end. About seventy men of Thaqif alone were killed and the Muslims took the enemy's riding camels, weapons and cattle. A party under Abu Amir al-Ash'ari pursued the fugitives to Awtas, where Abu Amir himself was killed. Horsemen who followed those running for Nakhlah caught Duraid bin as-Simmah, and he was killed by Rabi'ah bin Rafi' — the old man who had told them to leave the families out of it.

The count of what was taken: six thousand captives, twenty-four thousand camels, over forty thousand sheep, four thousand ounces of silver. All of it was gathered at al-Ji'ranah, put under Mas'ud bin Amr al-Ghifari, and left there undistributed.

Among the prisoners was ash-Shayma bint al-Harith as-Sadiyah, his foster sister from the years with Bani Sa'd. She named herself to him; he recognised her by a mark, spread his own garment on the ground for her to sit on, and sent her back to her people free.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih Muslim — the Companions answering 'here we are' as they turned back; Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Military Expeditions
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Revelation
layers.subtitle: Two verses that name what went wrong
layers.content:
The Qur'an records the day, and it does not record it as a victory story. It names the fault first.

«وَيَوْمَ حُنَيْنٍ إِذْ أَعْجَبَتْكُمْ كَثْرَتُكُمْ فَلَمْ تُغْنِ عَنكُمْ شَيْئًا وَضَاقَتْ عَلَيْكُمُ الْأَرْضُ ثُمَّ وَلَّيْتُمْ مُدْبِرِينَ» — 'and on the Day of Hunayn, when your great number pleased you and availed you nothing, and the earth, vast as it is, was straitened for you, then you turned back in flight.' (9:25)

Only after that does the verse of rescue come: «ثُمَّ أَنزَلَ اللَّهُ سَكِينَتَهُ عَلَىٰ رَسُولِهِ وَعَلَى الْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَأَنزَلَ جُنُودًا لَّمْ تَرَوْهَا» — 'Then Allah sent down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and sent down forces you did not see.' (9:26)

Read in order the two verses are a diagnosis followed by a treatment. The largest army the Muslims had ever assembled was routed inside an hour, and the reason given is not the ambush, not the terrain, not Malik's planning. It is that they had looked at their own numbers and been pleased.

The warning had already been given twice on that same road, and both times it was refused. A tree they wanted to keep, because other people had one. A sentence about not being defeated, spoken while the column was still intact. Neither was punished at the time. Both were answered in the valley.

The verses settled something the community would need for the rest of its history. Victory at Badr had come to three hundred and something men. Defeat at Hunayn came to twelve thousand. The variable being tested was never the headcount.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Siege, and What It Left Behind
layers.subtitle: A fort that held, and spoils that nearly split the army
layers.content:
Most of the beaten men went up to at-Ta'if with Malik bin Awf and shut the gates, so the Ta'if campaign is really the second half of Hunayn. Khalid bin al-Walid went ahead with a thousand men; the Prophet ﷺ came by Qarn al-Manazil and Laiyah, where he had Malik's castle pulled down, and camped under the walls.

How long the siege lasted is disputed; the reports place it between ten and twenty days. Arrows came off the wall like a swarm of locusts and twelve Muslims were killed, so the army pulled back out of range. A catapult opened a gap; men went through it under a wooden tank to set fires and had molten iron poured on them. The vines were ordered cut and burned, and the people inside begged for them by kinship. A crier announced that whoever left the fort was free, and twenty-three men came out.

The fort held over a year of provisions. Nawfal bin Mu'awiyah ad-Daili put it plainly: they are a fox in its den; wait and you take it, leave and it costs you nothing. He lifted the siege. The army hated going, so he let them fight one more morning, and after they were wounded they moved out willingly, which made him laugh. Asked to curse Thaqif, he said: O Allah, guide Thaqif, and bring them to us as Muslims.

At al-Ji'ranah he waited ten nights, then divided the spoils, and the largest shares went to recent enemies: a hundred camels to Abu Sufyan bin Harb, as much again for each of two sons, three hundred to Safwan bin Umayyah. The Ansar, who had turned back into the valley while others ran, got none of it. When their anger reached him he gathered them and asked whether they were unhappy that other men go home with ewes and camels while they go home with the Messenger of Allah. They wept into their beards.

Then fourteen men of Hawazin came as Muslims, chose their families over their property, and six thousand captives went home.

Carry this. He spent camels on the loyalty that had a price and spent none on the loyalty that did not, and he said so to their faces.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — the twenty-three men who came out of the fort, and the Prophet's address to the Ansar over the distribution at al-Ji'ranah
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

quiz.prompt: How many men marched out with the Prophet ﷺ to Hunayn?

options.text: Three thousand
Ten thousand, the same force that took Makkah
Twelve thousand — the ten thousand of the conquest plus two thousand more
Thirty thousand

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — Allah's Messenger leaves for Hunayn
quiz.scholar_reflection: Most of the extra two thousand were Makkans who had been polytheists a few weeks earlier. It was the largest force he had ever led, and its size is precisely what the Qur'an holds against it.

quiz.prompt: Who told Malik bin Awf to leave the women, children and property somewhere safe and fight with the young men only?

options.text: Duraid bin as-Simmah, the old war veteran
Nawfal bin Mu'awiyah ad-Daili
Safwan bin Umayyah
Zuhair bin Surad of Hawazin

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the war veteran disputes the leader's judgment
quiz.scholar_reflection: Malik called him senile and threatened to fall on his own sword. Duraid was killed in the pursuit after the battle he had refused to watch.

quiz.prompt: Whose voice was used to call the scattered army back to the Prophet ﷺ in the valley?

options.text: Khalid bin al-Walid's
Bilal's
Umar bin al-Khattab's
His uncle al-Abbas's

quiz.citation: Sahih Muslim, cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: Al-Abbas said they turned back like wild cows tending to their calves. The first hundred to reach him were enough to restart the battle.

quiz.prompt: How long did the siege of at-Ta'if last?

options.text: A single night
Reports differ — somewhere between ten and twenty days
Exactly forty days, agreed by all sources
Six months, until the fort ran out of food

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, citing Fath al-Bari — the length of the siege is a matter of disagreement
quiz.scholar_reflection: The sources do not settle it, and the book says so rather than choosing. What is agreed is that the fort was never taken and the army withdrew.

quiz.prompt: When the Hawazin delegation came as Muslims and were offered a choice, what did they ask for?

options.text: Their camels and silver, since the captives could be ransomed later
Their women and children — nothing compares with kinship
A share of the spoils equal to the Makkans'
The return of at-Ta'if to Malik bin Awf

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the arrival of the delegation of Hawazin
quiz.scholar_reflection: Six thousand captives were released. Not everyone agreed at first: al-Aqra' bin Habis and Uyainah bin Hisn both refused for their own tribes, and Uyainah held back one old woman before letting her go.

quiz.prompt: The largest shares of the Hunayn spoils went to men who had fought against him a month before. The Ansar, who had turned back into the valley when others ran, got nothing. How do you read that?

options.text: Resources belong where they will do most work, not where they are most deserved
It was unfair, and the Ansar were right to say so
He was buying stability in Makkah, and it was worth the price
The point was that the Ansar had already been paid in something else

quiz.slider_label: Reward the loyal — Win over the wavering
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the disturbed and uneasy state of the Helpers
quiz.scholar_reflection: He did not tell them their complaint was wrong. He gathered them privately, made the reasoning explicit, and asked whether they would rather have the camels. They chose him and wept.

quiz.prompt: Malik bin Awf put his people's wives and children behind the battle line so his men would have no choice but to fight. What do you think of that as a strategy?

options.text: Removing the option to retreat is the oldest way to guarantee effort
It gambled other people's lives on his own judgment
Duraid was right — fear does not stop a man who has already broken
It nearly worked; the Muslims did break first

quiz.slider_label: Bind them to the fight — Keep an exit open
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the enemy's march and their encampment at Awtas
quiz.scholar_reflection: It cost him six thousand captives, twenty-four thousand camels and forty thousand sheep in one afternoon. The advice he called senile would have cost him a battle only.

quiz.prompt: The verse says their own great number pleased them and availed them nothing. Where do you notice that in yourself — the quiet confidence that comes from size, support or resources?

options.text: I feel it most when things are going well, which is when it is hardest to see
Confidence in means is not the same as trusting them instead of Allah
Preparation is commanded; the fault was the pleasure, not the numbers
I recognise the opposite problem — I trust my means far too little

quiz.slider_label: Count your means — Discount your means
quiz.citation: Quran 9:25 — 'when your great number pleased you and availed you nothing'
quiz.scholar_reflection: The army at Badr was outnumbered roughly three to one and won. The army at Hunayn outnumbered its enemy and ran. Both outcomes are attributed in the Qur'an to the same cause, and it is not arithmetic.

quiz.prompt: He walked away from at-Ta'if without taking it, and when asked to curse the people inside he asked for their guidance instead. What does that tell you about how he measured the campaign?

options.text: The fort was never the objective; the people were
It was realism — the siege was costing more than it could win
A curse would have closed a door he intended to keep open
He could afford patience, and knew it

quiz.slider_label: Finish what you started — Leave the door open
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the invasion of at-Ta'if and the lifting of the siege
quiz.scholar_reflection: Thaqif came to Madinah as Muslims the following year, in Ramadan of 9 AH, and asked for terms. The unbroken siege did not stay unbroken.

quiz.prompt: For a few minutes in the valley almost nobody was left facing forward, and he pushed his mule at the enemy calling out his own name. What do you take from that image?

options.text: Someone has to stay in place before anyone else can come back
He was announcing his position to an enemy that wanted him dead
The reversal began with a voice, not with a weapon
It shows what he actually believed about the outcome

quiz.slider_label: Regroup and return — Hold the ground now
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the archers and the attackers stunned the Muslims
quiz.scholar_reflection: Two men were pulling at the mule to stop it going forward. His own uncle was one of them. The sirah calls this the moment his bravery was brought to light, and the rally started from where he was standing.
